Chapter 3 — The Temptation of Gradualism and the Trap of Revisionism.
Picture this: the protest’s over, banners put away, and the city feels strangely quiet. In a cozy café just off the square, a handful of activists sit huddled around a table. Their voices are soft, but there’s a current of energy under the surface. They’re talking about what comes next—what their movement should do now that the crowd’s gone home.
One person suggests focusing on the next election. Someone else brings up a campaign for better housing. There’s a sense of hope, but also, a cautious tone. It feels like everyone’s thinking, “Let’s not get ahead of ourselves.” Big dreams, sure, but maybe they need to be a little more realistic.
This is what gradualism looks like. It’s the idea that change happens slowly—step by step, through careful talks and a willingness to compromise. Sounds safe, right? It appeals to anyone who’s worried about risking too much, or afraid of pushing too hard and losing what’s already been gained. Gradualism promises progress without chaos, improvement without shaking things up too much.
But as the conversation unfolds, doubts start to creep in. Someone at the table points out that these promises—they’ve all been made before. And honestly, the results? They often don’t live up to the hope. Another activist wonders out loud if focusing so much on little wins has caused them to lose sight of the bigger picture.
Suddenly, there’s a realization: maybe, in trying to avoid conflict, they’ve drifted away from what originally brought them together.
That’s where the danger of revisionism comes in. It’s not always obvious, because it starts with good intentions. You want to win support, avoid alienating allies, or at least get something done—anything, really—rather than nothing. But over time, all those small compromises start to add up. Before you know it, the core ideas that made the movement powerful in the first place are fading into the background.
For anyone who’s poured their hope into gradual change, realizing this can sting. It means admitting the path might not lead where you dreamed it would go. It means facing the hard truth that, in trying to make the system just a bit fairer, you might have ended up keeping the very inequalities you set out to challenge.
See, the trap of revisionism isn’t just about strategy or tactics—it’s about vision. When your goal shifts from transforming the system to just making it a little more humane, the movement loses its spark. The dream of a world without exploitation is quietly swapped for the hope of a slightly softer version of the same old order.
As the activists step out of the café and into the night, some feel a spark of renewed purpose. They know the road ahead won’t be easy, but now they’re clearer on what’s truly at stake. Others feel discouraged, not sure which way to go next. Most, though, walk away with a mix of both feelings.
The temptation of gradualism is always there, but so is the deep, driving need for something more.
